package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of Spring Framework allow attackers to manipulate internal ClassLoader attributes via crafted POST requests, enabling remote code execution (RCE) by writing arbitrary files (such as web shells) to accessible locations on the server. This is due to insufficient parameter filtering and the ability to reach sensitive objects through class.module.classLoader.* parameters.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (HTTP POST request to a Spring endpoint accepting POJOs)
execution_context.file_location: Any Spring Web Controller endpoint that binds request parameters to objects

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code manipulates Tomcat's logging configuration via POST parameters to write a new file with a .jsp extension containing attacker-supplied code, resulting in a web shell being written to a web-accessible directory.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior allows external users to reconfigure server internals and write arbitrary executable files, which is a classic remote code execution vector.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Spring applications should not allow external input to modify internal server configuration or write files to arbitrary locations, especially not executable code.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate configuration changes should only be possible by trusted administrators through secure channels, not via user-facing HTTP endpoints.
key_indicators: Use of class.module.classLoader.* parameters in HTTP requests
Modification of Tomcat logging pipeline attributes via user input
Writing files with .jsp extension to web-accessible directories
Injection of attacker-controlled code into server-side files

attack_chain.action: Attacker identifies a POST endpoint in a vulnerable Spring application that binds request parameters to POJOs.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to send crafted POST requests to the server.

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a crafted POST request with class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.* parameters to reconfigure Tomcat's logging to write to a .jsp file in a web-accessible directory.
attack_chain.leads_to: Server is reconfigured to write attacker-controlled content to a new JSP file.

attack_chain.action: Attacker triggers a log event (e.g., another HTTP request) to cause Tomcat to write the malicious pattern (web shell code) into the new JSP file.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious JSP file containing web shell code is created on the server.

attack_chain.action: Attacker accesses the new JSP file via HTTP, executing the web shell and gaining remote code execution on the server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full remote code execution and potential server takeover.

behavioral_signatures: HTTP POST requests containing class.module.classLoader.* parameters
Unexpected changes to Tomcat logging configuration at runtime
Creation of new .jsp files in web-accessible directories
Execution of newly created JSP files shortly after configuration changes
file_indicators: webapps/ROOT/ohno.jsp (or other unexpected .jsp files in webapps/ROOT or similar directories)
Log files with .jsp extension containing web shell code
network_indicators: Unusual POST requests to Spring endpoints with suspicious parameter names
Subsequent HTTP GET requests to newly created .jsp files
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for HTTP requests containing class.module.classLoader.* parameters, especially those targeting Spring endpoints that bind request parameters to objects. Alert on creation of new .jsp files in web-accessible directories and on changes to Tomcat logging configuration at runtime. Correlate suspicious POST requests with subsequent execution of new JSP files.
